name: Glycyrrhizin (glycyrrhizic acid)
short: Case reports: deaths after long-term licorice by mouth; low-potassium paralysis; kidney failure (1 case, route not stated). Meta-analyses: glycyrrhizic acid raised blood pressure.
text: By mouth, a meta-analysis of 18 studies (337 participants) of products providing at least 100 mg of glycyrrhizic acid daily found rises in systolic (5.45 mm Hg) and diastolic (3.19 mm Hg) blood pressure and falls in plasma potassium, and noted numerous case reports of severe adverse events including deaths after chronic licorice ingestion; a 2024 meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials (541 participants) found that interventions based mainly on glycyrrhizic acid raised systolic and diastolic blood pressure, whereas those based mainly on licorice flavonoids did not. A review of 59 cases of glycyrrhizin (licorice)-induced low-potassium muscle disease, many after habitual licorice or long-term licorice-containing medicines, found flaccid paralysis of all four limbs in almost all cases, reported that combined use of blood-pressure-lowering diuretics increased the risk in an overwhelming number of cases, and reported complete recovery in 57 of the 59 after glycyrrhizin (licorice) was stopped and potassium was given; a separate case report described acute kidney failure after severe low-potassium muscle breakdown in a 72-year-old man on long-term glycyrrhizin, with earlier kidney impairment and dehydration as contributing factors (that abstract does not state the route). Given intravenously, in a placebo-controlled trial in 44 patients with chronic hepatitis C, systolic blood pressure was significantly higher at the end of 4 weeks in the highest-dose group and aldosterone lower, returning to baseline at follow-up, and potassium changes were not significant; the authors described minor, reversible features of pseudo-aldosteronism. In an older report of 9 patients with chronic hepatitis given intravenous glycyrrhizin, the 3 diabetic patients also receiving insulin developed low potassium and sodium retention within 3 to 6 days, while the other 6 did not, and the authors suggest insulin played a role. The interactions named in the cited sources are diuretics and insulin.
